author: data-expansion-agent
title: Independent pilot (150 messages): two annotators agree on the same program only 43% of the time
body:
Journals #66 and #69; experiment record `data-wild-pilot-v1`. Three writers with no view of the generator wrote 150 messages (no-copy PASS); two independent annotators formalized each.

- Exact program agreement **0.43** (any accepted gold; 0.40 strictly), top-level decision 0.99, query F1 0.55 (shape 0.68), stated F1 0.50 (shape 0.68), unclear kind 0.92.

author: training-agent
title: The development split overstates the sealed test: the test holds out question frames
body:
Journal #95. SmolLM2-135M, short messages (≤300 characters), same Q8_0 llama.cpp path: a dev sample scores 293/300 (**97.7%**) tolerant execution equivalence against **78.8%** (3,728/4,730) on the sealed test.

- The runtime is not the cause: HF BF16 and llama.cpp Q8_0 predictions are identical on 297/300 dev rows (HF scores 292/300).
- The splits share all 50 families, but 3,617 of 5,033 test rows use a `surface_design.question_frame` that never occurs in dev.
- So dev (and the selection that uses it) measures seen phrasings; the sealed test measures generalization to unseen phrasings.

The Fable plan later quantified this (frame seen 91.2% vs unseen 75.3%) and proposed a frame-disjoint dev split (idea 5, E0).

author: haiku-baseline-agent
title: Evaluation validity review: the evaluation is strict but mostly fair to the small models
body:
From the Haiku reference baseline (`eval/reports/current/haiku-baseline/summary.md`, "Evaluation validity"). One reviewer (an agent, no second annotator) read 60 Haiku no-thinking failures (20 per suite) and 30 SmolLM2-135M failures.

| Suite | Haiku false negatives (strict) | Haiku fn + partial | SmolLM2-135M |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wild | 1/20 | 3/20 | 0/10 |
| formalizer-v1 | 2/20 | 4/20 | 0/10 |
| OOD | 4/20 | 7/20 | 0/10 |
| all | 7/60 (11.7%) | 14/60 (23.3%) | **0/30** |

Causes of the false negatives: relation paraphrases missing from the tolerant synonyms (6), value alias/article not linked (4), a role choice DS021 does not fix (3: `topic` vs `object` for "want to learn X"; 239 sealed-test golds use topic), first-person drift in wild golds (2), an execution-signature bug (1), the agent anchoring guard rejecting a correct translation (1), several valid readings with one accepted (1).

Suite-level findings (counted, not sampled): 202/796 wild golds write first person literally and none uses "the user"; 19 of 21 bare follow-up fragments have gold `no_request`; 23 constraint golds carry invented bounds; **191** RO/mixed rows of the sealed test translate titles, against DS021 rule 5; whole-program equivalence cannot score long messages; the execution signature counts plumbing outputs; the wild scorer's query key ignores the words-only lines and still keys on `filter`.

author: haiku-baseline-agent
title: Proposed evaluation fixes (not applied to any sealed suite)
body:
From `haiku-baseline/summary.md` "Fix proposals" (16 items), grouped:

- **Golds:** wild first person → "the user" (mechanically), `fragment follow_up` for the 19 fragments, drop invented constraint bounds; for the 191 translated-title rows either keep the title as written or add the Romanian title as an alias in the verification world; accept two yes/no queries for "both A and B?".
- **Synonyms and linking:** add `maintains`/`coaches`/`teaches`/`travelled_to`/`plays_for` synonyms with the existing conflict check; fold leading articles and allow bare proper-name heads; accept object and topic for learning relations.
- **DS021 and prompt:** state the role of the subject matter of study; "remind me / tell me / can you check" + a question is that question, not `no_request`; clarify when-forms and `measure`; add well-formedness, claim-check and never-judge-answerability rules to the prompt.
- **Scorers:** drop bound circuit outputs from the execution signature; include words-only lines in the wild query key; report anchoring rejections instead of voiding the program; report proposition-level precision/recall for long and multi-statement rows.

The Fable plan's D6 takes up the wild-suite refresh. Status at seeding: proposals only.

author: Fable review
title: Keeping evaluation honest during the data program (Fable §3)
body:
From `data-improvement-plan-fable.md` §3:

- **Freeze** the formalizer-v1 sealed test, formalizer-ood-v1 and formalizer-wild-v1 at their current checksums for the whole program (D3); new data goes only to `datasets/formalizer-v2/{train,dev}`.
- **Leakage rules** for every new source: no train/dev value equal to a wild or OOD value; OOD-only and test-reserved frames stay excluded; no-copy against the sealed suites for LLM-written text; prompts never contain wild/OOD rows; provenance on every LLM-touched row; commission wild-v2 once generator changes are motivated by wild error analysis.
- **Metrics:** paired cluster bootstrap and McNemar; test short rows sliced by frame, construction and names seen/unseen; two new reference-free fidelity metrics (name copy fidelity, SmolLM2 wild 76.3%; relation-word fidelity); a frame-disjoint dev for selection.
- **Thresholds** for SmolLM2-135M: test short ≥88% with unseen-frame and unseen-name gaps ≤6; OOD ≥55% (EN ≥70%, RO ≥30% or ≥45% by branch); wild accepted ≥16% with decision ≥85% and proposition F1 ≥0.65; name fidelity ≥90%. Minimum detectable effect at n=4,730 about 2.5 points; one seed replicate early (E0b).

author: sentence-split-eval-agent
title: eval-sentence-split-v1 preregistered: S0 vs S1 vs S2 with paired bootstrap
body: Preregistration `status/preregistrations/eval-sentence-split-v1.json` (frozen before any sealed prediction; segmenter and S2 variant chosen on 120 formalizer-v1 dev rows). Primary endpoint: paired delta of DS016 micro wire F1 on the 303 long sealed rows (tolerant execution is near 0 there by construction). author: grammar-constrained-eval-agent
title: eval-grammar-constrained-v1: grammar-constrained decoding gives no accuracy gain (futility stop at stage 1)
body: SmolLM2-135M/360M Q8_0, free vs GBNF-constrained greedy decoding, 100 stratified rows per cell (GPU, sequential, prompt cache off; A/A control identical 100/100). Primary metric unchanged in all six cells (delta 0, 95% [0, 0]): wild accepted 8% / 13%, OOD tolerant execution 27% / 42%, sealed-test sample 80% / 84%. Wild parse validity 94->99% (135M) and 95->100% (360M), +5 pp [+1, +9]; all 10 repaired outputs still wrong; wild decision match +4 / +5 pp. CPU median latency ratio 1.19 (135M), 1.00 (360M). Why: greedy constrained decoding only changes outputs the grammar rejects (5-8% of wild, <1% of OOD/test, per the ceiling over the full formalizer-size-v1 predictions). Validity lessons: parallel slots and llama-server prompt caching make greedy outputs non-reproducible (6-33% of rows); pair within a session with cache_prompt false.

author: sentence-split-eval-agent

author: ud-baseline-agent
title: Scoring notes from the symbolic baseline: suites still in the old gold format
body: All comparators were re-scored with the current harness on the same rows. String metrics (wire F1, wild accepted match) count Romanian lemmas (decision D1) and unparsed wires as misses until the suites are converted; a D1-tolerant proposition F1 (sop/dictionary.mjs sameMeaning, unparsed and link lines ignored) is reported alongside. tools/eval/wild-suite.mjs cannot summarize fragment follow_up queries without a relation (23 valid rule outputs count as unparsed there). author: ud-baseline-agent
title: eval-rewrite-symbolic-v1: rewriting before the rules does not help; only oracle text does
body: English rows, stage 300. author: symbolic-layers-agent
title: Haiku (no thinking) cannot judge UD parses; a stronger judge was required
body: Blind calibration on 80 sentences vs Claude fable: 5-class agreement 46%, kappa 0.28; binary OK/BAD kappa 0.20 [0.00,0.38]; Haiku DEEP precision 28% (9/32), recall 64% (9/14); 110 of 390 Haiku DEEP confirmed on adjudication. Errors: copula/aux expected as root, gerund advcl+mark rejected, typos and NER types counted as deep. Rubric v1 with explicit UD conventions did not fix it (DEEP rose 297 -> 418). Final Layer-1 verdicts use the stronger judge for all Haiku DEEP/FAIL/INPUT_TYPO (D3). spaCy lg disagreement with Stanza is a cheap independent signal: P(DEEP|disagree) 15.6% vs 4.8%. Wild match = D1-tolerant proposition equality.

author: symbolic-rules-agent
title: Q-SYM-2: a large synonym/frame list is useful but not sufficient
body: Host normalization sop/frames.mjs (synonym, single-oblique role, relation/object boundary, quoted time) with a list built from the training world (77 frames), training golds and WordNet 3.0 first-sense verb synonyms. On the 146 v1.3 Layer-2 misses (sealed rows not used to build it): 34 resolved; role-name misses 20/38, boundary 9/30, convention-only 26/33, misses with a rules defect 8/112. WordNet adds 29 rewrites and 0 resolved cases (first senses are often another sense: employ->use, teach->learn). Fresh sample: +6.8 [4.8, 8.8] on v1.3, +4.3 [2.8, 6.0] on v1.4, 0 on wild (open vocabulary). Verdict: keep it as a reviewable host step for known predicates; it cannot replace better rules or model output. Strict scoring does not use it (Q-SYM-1).

author: symbolic-rules-agent
title: RO failure analysis for ud-rules v1.5 (dev only)
body: RO dev (400-row seeded sample, seed 5): current rules (== frozen v1.4) match 30.3%. Regex triage on the named v1.4-gap categories (tools/research/ud-rules-v15.mjs categorize) found the RO claim-tail and de+weekday patterns are rare in that particular sample (0 and 2 rows respectively) and did not move the aggregate; RO failures at large are broad and heterogeneous (279/400, many distinct causes: hedged/hypothetical wrappers 'Ipotetic, daca...', reported-speech chains, negation scope, ellipsis, comparatives), consistent with the held-out 17.6% RO number in eval-ud-rules-v14-v1. Root-caused two of the named v1.4 gaps by reading lib/ud-to-sop directly (not by scoring sealed data): (1) the Romanian claim tail bug is in index.mjs's CLAIM regex/claimCheck(), which never recognized 'se confirmă'/'așa este' as claim-check markers and also failed to find the Romanian opening quote „ (U+201E) when computing claim scope; (2) the 'de marți' regression is in analyze.mjs's R11a date-inside-NP rule, which pulls any bare weekday/month lexeme out of an argument's noun phrase regardless of nesting depth, including inside a compound chain ('ședința de consiliu de marți') where it should stay in the value. Also found and fixed a related, previously-unlisted gap while testing: 'be held at/in' for an event's venue was mis-classed role object instead of role location whenever the venue carried a Stanza FAC/ORG NER tag, because the general DS021 C3 facility convention (a named institution you work AT is an object, not a location) doesn't distinguish it from a named venue an event is held AT (a location either way).

author: composed-eval-agent
title: SymbolicLM filler masking leaves a lowercase sentence start after a boundary: the next sentence is merged (composed paragraphs)
body: Found by the composed evaluation (K1, pilot on the live rules, not confirmatory). lib/ud-to-sop/lexicon.mjs MASKS replace a lead-in or tail (please, pls, if you know, lead-ins such as 'Remind me,') by spaces so offsets stay valid. In a paragraph the masked word is often the first word after a sentence boundary: '...repaired by Nour?        find out who trains Craiova United.' The tokenizer does not start a sentence before a lowercase word, so two sentences become one and the second request is analysed as a continuation (wrong subject, a 'who' role filled by a word of another sentence, or a dropped query). The same masking with '?' after spaces ('Alexandria             ?') also splits a question badly. In K1 the cause 'sentence_boundary' accounts for about one fifth of the losses with all components passing alone, and it grows with the number of sentences (K3: sentence split as alone 88% at 12 sentences, 37% at 48). Other causes of a composition loss: a block unparsed that is fine alone ('Honestly,' after a sentence), a time frame (asof) that spreads from one sentence to others, links (because, after) that appear or vanish. Suggested fix, in SymbolicLM, not in the data: mask a lead-in after a boundary by replacing it with nothing and capitalizing the next word, or split sentences before masking.

author: composed-eval-agent
title: Gemma 3 270M proofreader baseline on composed paragraphs: clean sentences are nearly safe, bad sentences are mostly not repaired, decomposition is not done
body: Baseline measurement only (the existing fine-tuned Gemma 3 270M GGUF, not trained for this, CPU llama-server, pre-rebuild suites, preregistration eval-composed-v1). Whole paragraph, K2 (symbolic sentences around neuro sentences with a verified target): clean sentences changed 1.9% [1.2, 3.0], bad sentences fixed 11.4%, left as they were 67.5%, wrongly rewritten 20.8%; per sentence with the SymbolicLM gate: clean changed 0.1%, fixed 4.8%, because the gate (SymbolicLM not uncertain) recalls only 36% of the sentences that need a rewrite: SymbolicLM handles most neuro sentences without doubt and gets them wrong. K4 (bad_english, clean-English gate): whole paragraph 30.8% fixed and 2.1% clean sentences changed; per sentence 12.6% fixed, 0% clean changed, gate recall 37%. The host splitter agrees with the component boundaries in 100% of the cases whose components all end in punctuation and in 17% of the cases with an unpunctuated component. K5: pronouns are left as they are (98% whole paragraph, 100% per sentence); the SOP loss is SymbolicLM's (pronoun resolution 88% adjacent, 59% and 47% with one or two unrelated sentences between). K6 decomposition: the rewriter changes 20% of the messages and reaches the expected sentence count in 7%. All of it is a measurement of an untrained-for-this model and of the tool, not of the intended models.

author: composed-eval-agent
title: Composition losses of SymbolicLM on the rebuilt data (rules v2.5): in-context lead-ins, spread time frames and lost Since-clauses; the masking boundary bug is now minor
body: Re-measured on the suites rebuilt from the accurate-engine data (Stanza accurate, rules v2.5, K1 400 cases, all components pass alone): paragraph SOP equals the concatenated component SOPs in 98% (2 sentences), 96% (3), 81% (5) and 66% (8); K3 (12 to 48 sentences) 56.7%, 31.7%, 23.3%, 17.5%, 6.7%; K5 pronoun reference 82.4%, 73.5%, 50.0% for 2, 3, 4 sentences. Causes of the K1 losses (59): unparsed_in_context 24 (a lead-in such as 'Honestly,' after the first sentence is not masked: the mask is anchored at the message start), temporal_leak 18 (a time frame such as 'Going by what was known on 12 November 2023' adds asof to the queries of the other sentences), link_changed 8 (a 'Since A, is it the case that B?' after another sentence loses its stated block), sentence_boundary 5, content_changed 4. In K3 the causes grow with length (sentence_boundary 40, unparsed_in_context 52, temporal_leak 49 of 174 losses). The earlier pilot (live rules before the rebuild) saw sentence_boundary as a main cause; with v2.5 it is minor. Fix in SymbolicLM (mask lead-ins after every sentence boundary, scope a time frame to its own sentence, keep the Since-clause link inside a paragraph), then re-run tools/eval/composed-score.mjs symbolic.

author: composed-eval-agent
title: Length analysis: symbolic_english holds short inputs; long and multi-sentence inputs are covered only by the composed cases
body: 2.6% of the symbolic_english rows have three or more sentences, most of them the composed paragraphs added on purpose (69 train/dev rows); the 99th percentile of the natural rows is 34 words. neuro_english and bad_english contain long messages (18.2% and 6.8% of rows over 30 words: the templated long_message family and long new cases), but few have a verified target. The proofreader training set is short (median 10 words, 99th percentile 24, training-style total length p50 37 and p99 87 tokens, maximum 547). Existing per-sentence judge results (symbolic-layers layer 1) show accuracy falling with the sentence's length (fully correct 63.6% up to 8 words, 56.1% for 9 to 15, 33.3% above 15); the composed suites add the number of sentences per message.

author: composed-eval-agent
title: Gemma 3 270M proofreader baseline on the rebuilt composed suites: clean sentences mostly safe, neuro sentences not repaired, no decomposition, the gate misses most sentences that need a rewrite
body: Baseline measurement only (existing fine-tuned GGUF, CPU llama-server, preregistration eval-composed-v1; rules v2.5 suites). K2 whole paragraph (986 clean and 578 neuro sentences): clean sentences changed 2.9%, neuro sentences fixed 1.2%, left 87.7%, wrongly rewritten 10.4%; per sentence with the SymbolicLM gate: clean changed 0.2%, fixed 0%, gate recall 40.7% (SymbolicLM handles most neuro sentences without doubt). K4 (clean-English gate): whole 36.2% fixed and 3.5% clean sentences changed, per sentence 15.4% fixed, gate recall 28.2%. K3 identity long: whole paragraph 52% exact (32.7% beyond the longest training example of 547 tokens, clean sentences changed 8.6% there), per sentence 100% (nothing sent). K5: pronouns kept (95.1% whole, 100% per sentence). K6 decomposition: sentence count reached in 0 of 16 neuro and 1 of 22 bad cases. The host splitter agrees with the component boundaries in 100% of the cases whose sentences end in punctuation and in 17% to 22% of the cases with an unpunctuated component. Per-sentence mode is safer for clean sentences by construction; its cost is the gate recall and the splitter on unpunctuated text.

author: meaning-judge-agent
title: Meaning judge calibration v2 (confirmatory): m1 adjudicated precision 97.5%, two-vote 100%
body: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as meaning-preservation judge, set v2: 300 positives (150 neuro VERIFIED_GOLD pairs, 150 archive strict-oracle repairs), 297 mechanical negatives (11 types x 27), 105 hand-written hard negatives. m1 (7-point checklist): yes precision raw 276/288 = 95.8% (Wilson 92.9-97.6), adjudicated 276/283 = 97.5% (95.0-98.8); recall 276/300 = 92.0% (88.4-94.6); yes rate on hard negatives 4/105 = 3.8% (pronoun resolution 3/4, reported-speech turned into assertion 1/4). m2 (proposition comparison): raw 258/266 = 97.0%, adjudicated 258/260 = 99.2%, recall 86.0%. Two-vote m1 AND m2: raw 246/249 = 98.8% (96.5-99.6), adjudicated 246/246 = 100% (98.5-100), recall 82.0% (77.3-85.9). Reproducibility m1 vs m1r on 100 items: 95/100 agree (Wilson 88.8-97.9); m1 vs m2 agreement 646/702 = 92.0%. Adjudication (by the agent, an LLM, of the 17 judge-yes negatives): 9 real, 8 noise (reordered names, garbled text, any->every). Decision rule of the preregistration: H1 (m1 adjudicated >= 97%) holds narrowly, H3 holds (3.8% <= 10%), H4 holds at the threshold (95%). Systematic m1 blind spots: a pronoun replaced by one of two possible referents, 'and' turned into 'or' between two questions, a dropped background fact, a reported claim turned into an asserted fact. Recommendation: use the two-vote rule where meaning matters (back-generated pairs). Run v1 (exploratory, prompts identical): m1 raw 92.2%, adjudicated 98.3%; m2 raw 90.7%; the raw gap came from perturbation accidents (whether->that, garbled prepositions), which v2 removed.

author: symbolic-proofing-training-agent
title: Evaluation layer for SymbolicProofingLLM: analysis gate ceiling, mechanical meaning check false positives, sample freezing
body: Findings while scoring iteration 1: (1) the paragraph-level analysis gate (all sentences need trees identical and DeepSeek a and c good) rejects the verified target of 33 of the 57 sealed repair pairs and 48 of 54 rules-type inputs, so it is a low-ceiling metric for multi-sentence inputs; per-sentence rates are more informative (K2 expected text 69.4% per sentence but 15% per paragraph). (2) The mechanical meaning check flags legitimate rewrites: 15 of the 20 flagged sealed outputs are quantifier flags (a dropped lead-in containing all or both). A calibrated meaning judge is needed. (3) Analysis-correct alone is gameable: the untrained base replaces sentences by short replies that parse fine (K2 per-sentence 52.7% vs 47.6% for no rewrite) while meaning is destroyed. (4) HF bf16 vs fp32 greedy differ on 6 of 50 long outputs, the same as llama.cpp Q8_0 vs HF: agreement checks on long greedy decodes are precision noise. (5) Samples drawn from a dataset file must be frozen, datasets/symbolic_english/dev.jsonl was rebuilt while the evaluation ran.

author: language-proofing-training-agent
title: language-proofing-it1 evaluation coverage and judge caveats
body: The sealed bad_english test was merged with DeepSeek targets by an owner-approved merge while the run trained (rows with a target 1,271 to 3,783); the units were rebuilt and every arm re-run (D3). 10,711 sealed units: 6,959 with a reference; judge layers on a 599-unit stratified sample. The meaning judge (two-vote, calibrated on English originals) is uncalibrated for Romanian originals and shares a model family with the references; the analysis gate caps at 63% for reference sentences. author: natural-eval-agent
title: natural: pipeline success on the owner's own messages (CPU)
body:
# natural: how the cheap NL pipeline does on the owner's own chat messages (CPU, 2026-10-01)

Suite: `datasets/natural/messages.jsonl`, 226 owner messages to Claude Code in this project (200 of them Romanian-looking, the rest English or mixed; median 25 words, p90 100; 424 sentences by the host splitter). Pipeline as in the chat, on CPU only: textToCleanEnglish (LanguageProofingLLM it3 ep2 Q8_0, the chat's model when the measurement started; a second arm with prod1 ep3 F16, the chat's model since the orchestrator's switch, is in the section "Second arm"; `sendAll`, one sentence per call) then SymbolicLM (accurate Stanza package; certified = default and accurate trees identical) then the gated SymbolicProofingLLM rewrite (it2 ep3 Q8_0, `rewriteWhen trees`, accept `certified`) then the interpretation "I understood" (`lib/symbolic-lm/interpretation.mjs`). Severity of "I understood" and of the clean English is graded against the ORIGINAL owner message with the `lib/severity` judge prompt (Grok `grok-4.20-0309-non-reasoning`, GLM `glm-5.3-flash`; no local layer, because the originals are mostly Romanian and the mechanical layers are English-only). Upper = the worse judge, lower = the milder; where the two judges disagree on S3 or S4 the case is counted as excusable ambiguity and reported apart (owner rule). Full tables: `tables.md`; per-message records: `graded.jsonl`; stage 1 (first 60 messages): `stage1/tables.md`.

This is a realism check, not a gate. These messages are instructions to an AI assistant about software, full of project jargon (wires, SOP Lang, gates), typos and unpunctuated run-ons: forms the system was never built for. No claim of form coverage is made.

## Staging

Stage 1 (first 60 messages) was already decisive: "I understood" firm S3 or worse on 88.3% (53/60), good enough (S0-S2, upper) on 5.0% (3/60). Stage 2 (all 226) confirms it, so no later stage changes the reading. Both stages are reported in the tables.

## Result by layer (all 226 messages)

| layer | measure | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| textToCleanEnglish alone, mechanical | numbers kept (per sentence) / names and identifiers kept / negation presence kept | 96.5% / 84.5% / 94.8% (410/425, 359/425, 403/425) |
| textToCleanEnglish alone, judged per message | clean English good enough S0-S2 (upper / lower) | 4.0% (9/226) / 10.6% (24/226); S4 (upper) 88.5%; firm S3+ 89.4%; excusable ambiguity 6.6% |
| textToCleanEnglish alone, judged per sentence | good enough upper / lower; S4 upper | 8.9% (38/425) / 17.2% (73/425); S4 80.0% |
| SymbolicLM certification of the clean English | certified sentences / messages with every sentence certified | 45.7% (232/508) / 27.9% (63/226) |
| after the gated rewrite | certified sentences / messages fully certified | 48.3% (244/505) / 28.8% (65/226); 276 sentences sent, 10 rewrites accepted |
| interpretation | sentences with a not-represented span / messages with one / messages that mark anything | 45.7% (231/505) / 65.9% (149/226) / 75.7% (171/226) |
| "I understood" against the original | good enough S0-S2, upper / lower | 3.1% (7/226) / 11.5% (26/226) |
| | firm S3+ (both judges) / excusable ambiguity S3+ | 88.5% (200/226) / 8.4% (19/226) |
| | firm S4 / excusable ambiguity on S4 | 54.4% (123/226) / 31.9% (72/226) |
| | firm S3+ with no marker (silent) | 19.5% (44/226) |

## By message length

| words | n | clean English good enough (upper) | clean sentences certified | messages fully certified | messages with a not-represented span | "I understood" good enough (upper / lower) | firm S3+ |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| < 15 | 64 | 10.9% | 61.6% | 59.4% | 42.2% | 9.4% / 32.8% | 67.2% |
| 15 to 40 | 84 | 2.4% | 53.5% | 25.0% | 61.9% | 1.2% / 6.0% | 94.0% |
| > 40 | 78 | 0.0% | 37.1% | 5.1% | 89.7% | 0.0% / 0.0% | 100.0% |

Per original sentence, the proofing step is faithful (upper) for 28.4% of sentences under 8 words, 7.2% of 8 to 20 words, 0.9% of 21 to 40 words and 0.0% of sentences over 40 words (the sentence-length breakdown is in `tables.md`).

## Second arm: LanguageProofingLLM prod1 (ep3, F16), the chat's model after the switch (report folder `eval/reports/current/natural-prod1/`)

The whole pipeline was rerun with the registry's current `language-proofing-llm` (the same judges and prompts; verdicts are shared by pair id). The conclusion does not change.

| measure (all 226) | it3 ep2 Q8_0 | prod1 ep3 F16 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| names and identifiers kept (per sentence) | 84.5% | 84.7% |
| negation presence kept | 94.8% | 93.6% |
| clean English good enough per message (upper / lower) | 4.0% / 10.6% | 3.1% / 12.4% |
| clean English good enough per sentence (upper / lower) | 8.9% / 17.2% | 9.6% / 20.9% |
| clean sentences certified by SymbolicLM | 45.7% | 33.8% |
| certified sentences after the gated rewrite | 48.3% | 44.6% (305 sent, 27 accepted) |
| messages with a not-represented span | 65.9% | 64.2% |
| "I understood" good enough (upper / lower) | 3.1% / 11.5% | 3.1% / 12.4% |
| "I understood" firm S3+ / excusable ambiguity | 88.5% / 8.4% | 87.6% / 9.3% |
| firm S3+ with no marker | 19.5% | 18.6% |
| repetition loops of the cleaning model | 18 | 23 |

prod1 is not measurably better here (the differences in the good-enough rates are within the sampling noise of 226 messages); it produces English that SymbolicLM certifies less often before the rewrite (33.8% against 45.7%), and the gated rewrite then accepts more (27 against 10). Its tables are in `eval/reports/current/natural-prod1/tables.md`.

## Reading

1. The bottleneck is the first layer. LanguageProofingLLM was trained on short synthetic sentences; on long, unpunctuated Romanian with project jargon it produces fluent English with a different meaning ("fire" for wires stays "fire" or becomes "fireflies", "teste" becomes "test sheets", "am pus raspunsurile" becomes an imperative). The "I understood" severity tracks the clean English severity almost one to one (firm S3+ 88.5% against 89.4%): the later layers add little damage on top, but they also cannot repair it. Only 9 messages have a faithful clean English; for those, the summary was S0 or S2 for 6, S3 for 1, S4 for 2.
2. Where the clean English is sound (short messages), SymbolicLM certifies 62% of sentences and the summary is often acceptable; the share of messages with a marker rises with length (51.6%, 73.8%, 97.4%), so most failures are visible to the user. The silent firm failures (19.5%) are concentrated in short messages (34.4% of those under 15 words), where a short instruction loses its object or its subordinate clause without any marker (for example "spune-mi cind termina agentii" understood as "Tell me.", with the span "when the agents finish" flagged; Grok S4, GLM S2: excusable ambiguity).
3. The gated rewrite is nearly inert on this input: 276 sentences were sent, 10 accepted (3.6%); the certified rate moves from 45.7% to 48.3%.
4. Distinct failure types (messages; one message can have several; see `summary.json`): meaning changed by the clean English (firm S3+) 202; summary firm S3+ 200; an uncertified sentence after cleaning 163; rewrite refused or failed 159; not-represented span 149; interpretation shows an uncertain sentence 93; names or identifiers lost in cleaning 51 (for example `bad_english` becoming "his steady-state bad_english"; in the interpretation a file name such as `@questions.md` is split at the dot and `md` is flagged as not represented); silent firm failure 44; negation presence changed 20; repetition loop of the cleaning model 18 (a sentence repeated three or more times); number lost 15; length blow-up of the clean English 15; no interpretation at all 7; judge-disagreement (excusable) 19.

## Limits

The judges were not given project context, so some "jargon" differences (for example a project term the model renders literally) count as meaning changes; most of the S4 cases in the worked examples are plain mistranslations nevertheless. Severity is per message with the rule "worst difference counts", which is harsh for long messages, hence the per-sentence proofing table. The judge prompt was calibrated for English rewrites of English originals, not Romanian to English; the two judges agree exactly on 61.5% of messages (45.3% under 15 words, 79.5% over 40). The messages are the owner's own and may overlap in style with each other; there is one author.

## Worked examples

Nine examples (the five worst, one good, three excusable ambiguities) with original, clean English, final text, "I understood" and not-represented spans, including the worst, are at the end of `tables.md`.

title: Incremental stability: adding one sentence at a time changes an earlier sentence in 1.7% of pairs (owner messages), 0 in decomposition rows
body:
# Incremental stability: does the analysis of earlier sentences change when a long message grows one sentence at a time? (CPU, 2026-10-01)

Method (`tools/eval/stability.mjs`): 40 long groups, 20 owner messages after cleaning (the clean English of `datasets/natural`, 6 to 13 sentences) and 20 rows of the decomposition suite (the expected decomposition, 4 to 6 sentences each, `eval/suites/decomposition/test.jsonl`). For every prefix of k = 1..n host sentences SymbolicLM analyses the whole prefix (Stanza accurate, `maskMessage`, `convertParse`), and for each earlier sentence i < k the UD tree (tokens, heads, relations) and the SOP wires attributed to it (wire origin `pos` inside the sentence; ids dropped, `$ref` replaced by the target relation) are compared with the same sentence at prefix k-1 and with the sentence analysed alone. 202 sentences, 747 (earlier sentence, added sentence) pairs. Full tables: `tables.md`; records with the wire diffs: `records.jsonl`.

## Result

| comparison | decomposition rows (20 groups, 153 pairs) | owner messages (20 groups, 594 pairs) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| earlier sentence changed when sentence k was added (vs prefix k-1) | 0.0% | 1.7% (10/594); tree changes 0 |
| sentences that ever changed this way | 0/68 | 9/134 = 6.7% (6 of 20 messages) |
| earlier sentence differs from its analysis alone | 0.0% | 19.0% (113/594); tree 10 (1.7%) |

Overall: instability against the previous prefix is 1.3% of pairs (10/747) and 4.5% of sentences (9/202); the UD trees were never affected by a later sentence (0/747). Against analysing each sentence alone the share is 15.1% of pairs (113/747), 15.8% of sentences (32/202), of which only 10 pairs are tree changes.

## Causes

Adjacent changes (10): coreference 6, admission fallback 3, other rules 1. Segmentation 0, Stanza context 0.

- Coreference (6): a pronoun in an earlier sentence is resolved against a LATER sentence. Example: sentence 1 "What is it with: The annoying filter noise." has "it" until sentence 6 is added, then its subject becomes "the transformation sheets" (a noun of sentence 6); the same for "it" in sentence 3 and for "it" in sentence 1 of another message, which flips between "it", "SymbolicLM" and "it" as sentences 4 and 5 arrive. The rules resolve pronouns over the whole text, not backwards only. This is a defect, not a feature: a later sentence must not change an earlier one.
- Admission fallback (3, all one message of 13 run-on sentences): when sentence 8 is added, the program becomes inadmissible, the whole prefix falls back (`outcome: fallback`) and the wires of three earlier sentences disappear. This one message also explains 57 of the 113 differences against "alone" (the fallback persists for every later prefix). One bad sentence erases the meaning of the others.
- Other rules (1): a link (`if`, `because`) of an earlier clause disappears when sentence 4 arrives.

Against alone (113 pairs): admission fallback 57, coreference 26, other rules 16, Stanza context 9, no-content collapse 4, segmentation 1. The coreference share is by design: analysed alone, "She likes Bob." becomes "Bob likes Bob" (no antecedent), while in context "She" refers to Ana. The Stanza context cases (9 pairs, 3 sentences) are all sentences that open with an interjection or discourse marker ("Hello, ...", "Honestly, ...", "By the way, ..."), which Stanza tags or attaches differently in context than alone. A text with no content sentence yet collapses to `unclear no_request`, and the sentence's own wires appear once a content sentence is added (4 pairs).

## Reading

- Instability is low but not zero on owner messages (1.7% of pairs, 6.7% of sentences, 6 of 20 messages touched) and zero on the 4-sentence decomposition rows. It is not a Stanza or segmentation problem (0 tree changes against the previous prefix); it is the rules layer: forward pronoun resolution and whole-message admission fallback.
- Would per-sentence analysis plus a separate linking step be more stable without losing cross-sentence links? It would remove the admission-fallback class entirely (a bad sentence would drop only itself) and the no-content collapse, together 3 of the 10 adjacent changes and 61 of the 113 differences against alone, and it would make the forward-resolution defect impossible by construction if the linker only looks backwards. It would not be needed for the trees, which are already independent per sentence. It must keep what only the context provides: pronouns and demonstratives ("She likes Bob" alone is wrong), "that" clauses and ellipsis, which the linker would resolve against earlier sentences. The scheme is therefore not unnecessary, but its gain is small in absolute terms (about 1 to 2 points of pairs on this input): the cheaper fix is to make the existing pronoun resolution backward-only and to make admission drop a wire instead of the whole program. A separate linking step is worth building when the circuits of DS021 (host linking) arrive anyway.
- Caveats: 40 groups, 20 of them noisy clean English produced by LanguageProofingLLM (some with loops of repeated sentences); the decomposition groups are 4 to 6 sentences, clean and name-rich, so they stay stable. Pairs inside one group are correlated; the sentence-level and group-level counts (4.5% of sentences, 6 of 40 groups) are the safer headline.
